extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of literature, history, and intellectual/philological lectures
extracted.subtask_description: Critical-essay style evaluation of 'Great Men', myths, and prophetic figures (e.g., Odin, Thor, Mahomet), extracting qualities that make heroic/prophetic figures and how cultures receive them. Focuses on traits like valor, sincerity, originality, and the cultural contexts that shape myth and religion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consecration of Valor (Norse Religion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Norse Religion as a 'Consecration of Valor' — Odin taught his people the infinite importance of Valor, by which man became god; Valor is primary and formative for the Norse world-view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This valor-seed produces the whole mythic growth (songs, sagas, rites). Evaluate Norse material for its emphasis on robust homely vigor, honest pity, and martial virtue (examples: Thor's physicality, Balder's death, Hermoder's ride). Anti-patterns: treating Norse myth as theatrical sublimity or aesthetic gloom (Gray/Pope-like misreadings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Seed-origin model of myth
rubrics_metrics.description: A single influential figure or 'seed' (a man speaking with a hero's voice) can generate an entire tree of traditions: myths, sagas, symbolic practices, songs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Banyan-tree metaphor: the first seed is essential; every branch that strikes root becomes a new center of growth. In evaluation, trace large mythic systems back to a formative charismatic source or message rather than treating them as monolithic ungenerated wholes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Norse poetic character: robust simplicity and directness
rubrics_metrics.description: Norse mythic poetry is rough, hearty, homely, with a tint of good humor and robust mirth; it favors veracity and direct conceptions over theatrical sublimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing Norse-style narrative or mythic writing, prize plain, vivid concreteness (e.g., 'knuckles grow white') and earthy details over affected grandeur. Examples: Thor's straightforward rage, Thor's manual labor (Thialfi), Hymir pot episode. Critique works that impose ornate, classical polish (Gray/Pope) which mask the native character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perennial truth preserved by tradition
rubrics_metrics.description: Old songs and myths endure because they embody an inward, perennial truth and greatness; this truth is not mere physical largeness but a 'rude greatness of soul'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate traditional/folk narratives by their capacity to express enduring existential insights (melancholy, meditation on the world's apparent illusoriness). Examples: Hamlet as a twig of the Norse world-tree; lines like 'We are such stuff as Dreams are made of!' mark this inward truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegory/play vs prophetic/devout distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Some mythic episodes belong to an allegoric or playful phase (e.g., Utgard/Skrymir story) rather than to the prophetic/devout core; forms shift over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate whether a myth functions as earnest prophecy, symbolic allegory, or later poetic play. This affects interpretation: allegory may be humorous or ironic, prophetic material should be read for deep religious/ethical import.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor grounded in earnestness and sadness
rubrics_metrics.description: A genuine heroic or mythic humor rests on earnestness and sadness (a 'Brobdignag grin of true humor'), not mere levity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In creative evaluation, value humor that emerges naturally from a serious imaginative engagement (examples: Skrymir episodes, Ben Jonson-like grim humor) rather than flippancy. Such humor indicates the moral and emotional depth of the tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ragnarok as law of mutation (death→rebirth)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Ragnarok myth embodies the idea that universal destruction and death are followed by renewal: 'all death is but a phoenix fire-death, and new-birth into the Greater and the Better.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat apocalyptic or cyclical endings as expressions of a philosophical law of change; assess mythic or literary works for whether catastrophe is presented as final annihilation or as transformative renewal.

rubrics_metrics.name: The reception of a Great Man reveals an epoch's spiritual condition
rubrics_metrics.description: How a society welcomes or interprets a Great Man (as god, prophet, genius, etc.) is the most significant feature of that epoch and shows its spiritual health or defects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing portraits of leaders/heroes, examine public reception and cult (deification, prophetic status, aestheticization). Examples: Scandinavians deifying Odin vs. modern reception of Burns as trivializing genius — both reveal cultural failures or virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity as the primary characteristic of the Great Man
rubrics_metrics.description: A deep, genuine sincerity (not the boastful 'sincerity' that is self-congratulating) is the foundational trait of any heroic figure; the Great Man 'cannot help being sincere'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating heroic figures in literature or history, foreground their authentic inner conviction and compulsion by the 'Fact of Existence' over rhetorical performance or calculated ambition. Distinguish true sincerity from conscious claims to sincerity or mere self-confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality/revelation: the Great Man as first-hand messenger
rubrics_metrics.description: A Great Man comes 'at first-hand' from the unknown; his utterances are like revelation because they spring from direct communion with primal reality rather than hearsay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess originality by the degree to which the speaker's voice feels immediate and grounded in lived perception rather than derivative. Consider whether speech/poetry functions as a revelation to others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inner struggle and repentance trump outward faults
rubrics_metrics.description: Outward faults of a hero are less decisive than the presence of genuine remorse, repentance, and ongoing moral struggle; the worst fault is consciousness of no sin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging moral or religious figures, focus on their inner moral trajectory (remorse, repentance, persistence) rather than cataloguing external transgressions. Biblical David used as exemplar: sins do not negate prophetic value if followed by true repentance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environment and culture shape charismatic character
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical environment and cultural institutions (e.g., Arabian deserts, Bedouin life, poetic contests) predispose a people and their leaders to particular heroic qualities (meditative, swift, eloquent, hospitable but fierce).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextualize the emergence of heroes/prophets within geography, social institutions (pilgrimage, fairs), and pre-existing cultural habits. Evaluate how well a depiction or account links character to environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sacred objects and pilgrimage as social-religious focal points
rubrics_metrics.description: Objects and sites (the Black Stone, Well Zemzem, the Caabah) create shared religious practice and social cohesion, forming centers from which religious movements and fairs/trade grow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In historical or fictional worldbuilding, give weight to tangible sacred foci and pilgrimage practices as mechanisms for communal identity and commercial/political consolidation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education/background (lack of formal schooling) as a factor in originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Absence of formal book-learning (e.g., Mahomet's lack of writing ability) can be a formative factor: a leader's desert-life education made him original and dependent on direct perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing authors/figures, consider whether lack of formal education contributes to authenticity and immediacy of vision rather than being an automatic deficiency. Account for how experiential knowledge substitutes for books.
